notes:
I've written notes for most of Jeremiah 31, but there are gaps. I ran out of searches and page reads. The Enduring Word page cut off after v. 19, and the Precept Austin and Matthew Henry pages loaded only their menus, not the commentary itself.

**What I couldn't find, so it's left out:** anything on vv. 21 and 23–26; anything from Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Pentecostal (ag.org, pneumareview.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) sites; netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org notes (only a short NET quote reached me through Precept Austin); and anything on hyper-grace, prosperity or word-of-faith readings. My one search on hyper-grace and v. 34 returned only Bible translations and standard sermons.

---

**v. 1:** Guzik ties "at that time" to "the latter days" of 30:24. He reads the verse as a future turning of Israel to God and the Messiah, and links it to Romans 11:26 ("all Israel will be saved"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/

**v. 2:** Guzik connects the survivors to "the time of Jacob's trouble" (30:7; Revelation 12). Most of those who survive will find grace and rest in Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/

**v. 3:** Guzik says God's love here reaches from eternity past to eternity future. He criticises Christians who think God has withdrawn that love from Israel as a nation. He also applies the love to every believer, quoting F. B. Meyer. Quoting Spurgeon, he notes that God draws people by love rather than fear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/

**vv. 4–6:** Guzik: God's loyal love means Israel will surely be rebuilt, with joy and plenty. The watchmen who once warned of enemies will instead call pilgrims up to Zion (he cites Thompson). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/

**v. 7:** Guzik: the news is too good to keep inside Israel. The whole earth should hear it and praise God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/

**v. 8:** Guzik reads "there" as a return to the land itself, not just to God. He calls the founding of Israel in 1948 a miracle, but says the promise is only fully kept when Israel comes to faith in the Messiah. His one-line summary stresses the literal land, not just a spiritual restoration. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/

**v. 9:** Guzik links the weeping and pleading to Zechariah 12:10, and quotes Spurgeon's 1855 belief that the Jews would return to their land. On "Ephraim is My firstborn," he notes Ephraim wasn't Jacob's firstborn, so "firstborn" means first place, not birth order. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/

**vv. 10–12:** Guzik: the nations must hear this message. "Ransom" and "redeem" carry ideas from commercial law and from family duty (Thompson). The "well-watered garden" means plenty for both body and soul. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/

**vv. 13–14:** Guzik: the priests have plenty because a blessed people bring large offerings (Harrison). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/

**v. 15 (Rachel weeping):**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik calls this a poetic image. Rachel, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, weeps from Ramah, near her grave, over her children taken into exile. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/
- Desiring God describes the Lord in effect bringing Rachel back to life to picture an Israelite mother weeping for her children. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/because-they-are-no-more
- Ellicott adds that "Rachel" means "ewe," so the picture is a ewe crying for her lambs. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/31-15.html
- **How Matthew uses it (a real difference in emphasis):**
  - Harrison (quoted by Guzik) says Matthew 2:18 cites the verse as a type (a pattern), not as a prediction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/
  - Coffman sees one prophecy with a near and a far fulfilment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/2-18.html
  - Gill takes Rachel to stand for the Bethlehem mothers, and treats Matthew's use as a fulfilment. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nrs/jeremiah/31-15.html
  - Ligonier says Matthew cites it as fulfilled in Herod's massacre. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/herod-slays-children

**vv. 16–17:** Guzik: God comforts the one who refuses comfort. That comfort has substance, because the children really will come back (he quotes Ryken: sorrow doesn't get the last word). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/

**vv. 18–19:** Guzik: Israel accepts its troubles as God's discipline, not blind fate. "Restore me, that I may return" shows complete dependence on God. Kidner: Ephraim now mourns his sins, not just his fate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/

**v. 20:** Not reached in any source I could read; the Enduring Word page cut off just before it.

**v. 22 ("a woman will shelter a man"):** This is the main point of disagreement between traditions.
- **Church fathers and some Protestants:** Augustine and almost all the Christian fathers read it as Mary carrying Christ in her womb. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/31-22.htm
  - Gill reads it the same way. The Geneva notes give the Virgin birth as one option, and Jerusalem becoming fruitful again as another. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/31-22.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** He says Christians adopted the Marian reading almost unanimously, partly from eagerness to find their salvation here. He prefers a different reading: weak Israel, like a woman, will overcome strong enemies. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom20/calcom20.iii.xxx.html
- **Other Protestant readings:** The Pulpit Commentary: Israel, the Lord's bride, will eagerly embrace her divine husband, though it admits the phrase is "extremely difficult." https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/31-22.htm
  - Keil links the verse to a new relationship between Israel and God, the new covenant of v. 31. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/31-22.htm
- **Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia lists Jeremiah 31:22 as a prophecy about Mary. It cites Jerome and Athanasius, says this meaning fits the text and its context, and rejects the "woman protects a man" reading. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15464b.htm

**vv. 29–30 (sour grapes):** Adam Clarke: no child is punished by God for a father's sin, unless he does the same things. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_31_commentary
- Matthew Henry: the saying was unfair to God, and God promises to stop his quarrel with them over their fathers' sins. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_031.cfm (This comes from a search preview of that page.)
- Ellicott notes that Ezekiel likewise puts the "new heart" promise right after his attack on this same saying. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/31-31.htm

**vv. 27, 31, 38 ("the days are coming"):** Precept Austin says the phrase occurs three times. It introduces in turn a restored nation, a new covenant and a rebuilt city, all in the Messiah's future reign from Jerusalem. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_31_commentary

**vv. 31–32 (new covenant):**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Guzik: a new covenant was needed because Israel didn't and couldn't keep the Sinai covenant, which was only preparation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/
  - Keil: the Sinai covenant's weakness was that people could break it, and the new one removes that weakness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/31-31.htm
  - Calvin: God made the new covenant when Christ fulfilled what the Law had only pictured, together with the Spirit's gift of new birth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/31-31.html
- **Who it is made with (a real disagreement):**
  - Guzik says it is first with Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/
  - Benson says its benefits actually went only to Abraham's spiritual descendants, the "Israel of God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/31-31.htm
  - MacLaren says Christians may apply "the house of Israel" to themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/jeremiah-31.html
- **How "new" is it? (Reformed view):** Ligonier: the Hebrew word can mean "brand new" or "a new edition," and the Greek Old Testament chose the word for "new edition." https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/new-covenant-2
  - Richard Pratt: the word means "renewed," so it is not an entirely new covenant. https://www.ligonier.org/learn/articles/out-old-and-new
  - Ligonier also teaches that Christ began the new covenant at his first coming and will complete it at his return. https://learn.ligonier.org/guides/covenant-theology

**vv. 33–34 (law on the heart; all will know me):**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Guzik: the new covenant brings a change on the inside. It doesn't cancel God's law; it brings the law closer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/
  - Spurgeon: it is pure grace, made with Christ as our representative, who has already kept the human side. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/jeremiah-31.html
  - A sermon collected on Bible Hub: God can't literally forget anything, but as judge he no longer holds the forgiven person's sins against them. https://biblehub.com/sermons/jeremiah/31-34.htm
  - Gill: forgiveness existed before, but only through symbols. Forgiveness is the main blessing of this covenant. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/jeremiah/31-34.html
- **Infant or believer's baptism (Baptist vs. Reformed):**
  - A Gospel Coalition essay argues that everyone in the new covenant has the law on their heart, so the church is a born-again community and baptism is for believers only. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/water-baptism/
  - A Reformed Baptist article asks whether "all" means every kind of person; the excerpt I saw doesn't show its conclusion. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/the-abrahamic-covenant-in-reformed-baptist-perspective/
  - Desiring God argues that every new-covenant believer is born again and fully forgiven, criticising covenant theology. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/dispensational-or-covenantal
  - Sam Storms agrees that this passage pictures the church as wholly born again. https://www.samstorms.org/enjoying-god-blog/post/a-brief-defense-of-believers-baptism
- **Other views:** Adam Clarke saw the verse fulfilled in his own day of Bibles, Sunday schools and village preaching. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/jeremiah/31-34.html
  - Bridgeway: people will no longer need priests to stand between them and God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/31-31.html

**vv. 35–37:** Guzik: God promises with cosmic seriousness never to reject Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/
- MacLaren: the sun, moon and stars serve as God's guarantee of his faithfulness, and the promises extend to Christians. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/jeremiah-31.html
- Matthew Henry applies the promise to Abraham's spiritual descendants. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_031.cfm (From a search preview.)

**vv. 38–40:** Guzik takes this as a literal, larger Jerusalem. The specific landmarks, he says, rule out a purely symbolic reading. He quotes another writer (the snippet doesn't say who) arguing it can't mean the city rebuilt after the exile, because this city is larger and will never be torn down. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-31/
